# Card 014 — 1st Special Forces Operational Detachment-Delta (Delta Force) at full commitment, under a newly formed MACV joint special operations command from August 1964

*Memorandum 014 · status part2 · full record: memos/014/ · generated by fie.py*

## P014a · 1st Special Forces Operational Detachment-Delta (SFOD-D, Delta Force), US Army, in its 2026 configuration and at full strength: the whole unit committed to Vietnam, with its assault squadrons, its reconnaissance and surveillance squadron, its organic aviation squadron and its support squadrons, without the wider JSOC package (no 160th SOAR, no dedicated JSOC ISR wing); missions: hunting PAVN and VC leadership and the infrastructure, COSVN and the base areas, POW recovery, raids into the North and reconnaissance, across the borders only where and when history's forces went
the whole unit, full commitment [U]; ~1,000–1,500 personnel of whom ~250–350 operators [E: open-source estimates of Delta's strength, D1] · spaces ~1,000–1,500 [E: the whole unit; no ceiling (CONFIG troop_ceiling = NONE)] · arrives 1964-09-01 · FIND, FIX, STRIKE, SUBVERT · ground

**Key figures.**
- Unit: established 19 November 1977 [M014·S1]; 2026 strength about 1,000–1,500, of whom about 250–350 operators [E: S1's 2001 figures grown by D Squadron and the support squadron]
- Organisation: four assault squadrons (two assault troops and a reconnaissance troop each; assault troop four teams of 5–6), G Squadron (advanced force), E Squadron (company of light helicopters and King Airs), signal and support squadrons [M014·S1] [M014·S2]
- Arrival 1 September 1964; headquarters 15 August 1964 [E: two weeks after the Tonkin reports]
- Borders as history: Laos from 18 October 1965 within the ambassador's limits; Cambodia from September 1967, foot reconnaissance only; the North only at Son Tay, 21 November 1970 [M014·S3] [M014·S5] [U]
- Raids in the South at maturity: about 40–120 a month; 15–35% reach a listed cadre at district level or above; about 80–400 such cadre a year [E: D5]
- Reconnaissance: 15–25 teams in the field at once, 40–80 team-missions a month [E: D5]; SOG's benchmark 454 Cambodian missions in 1969 [M014·S3]
- Replacement: about 30–50 operators a year from selection and the six-month OTC [E: S1]
- 2026 equipment stock about two to three years of wastage; thinning from 1966–68 [E: D8]
- History's benchmarks: JPRC never recovered an American POW (8 and 9 successes in 1968–69, 272 Vietnamese recovered) [M014·S6]; Son Tay empty, prisoners moved 14 July 1970 [M014·S5]; SOG's northern agents more than three-quarters captured [M014·S3]

**Negative specification.** Delta cannot find what no one has found. It finishes targets that the combined task force, the U-2S and Global Hawks, a defector or a captured document have located [M012] [M003]; it locates very little itself beyond the reach of its own patrols, and nothing under triple canopy from the air. It cannot destroy a main-force unit: a battalion of 400 is not a raid target for a troop of 20–24 operators [E: D2]. It cannot reach COSVN by raid while COSVN is in Cambodia, because no American ground force crosses that border until September 1967, and then only on reconnaissance on foot without air support, and with no exploitation force [M014·S3]; and COSVN, about 2,400 staff dispersed and mobile, evaded Junction City, Menu and the 1970 incursion [M014·S7]. It cannot raid the North before history's one raid at Son Tay in November 1970 [M014·S5]. It cannot enter Laos before October 1965 [M014·S3]. It brings no 160th SOAR and no drone orbit of its own [U]: its lift is a company of light helicopters [M014·S2], and any operation larger than a troop or deeper than their range needs the theater's lift. It cannot speak Vietnamese, so every target that comes through Vietnamese hands comes with the risk of a leak. It cannot be handed to the ARVN, and its 2026 equipment cannot be repaired in 1964 (D8). And it is not numerous: about 280–350 people who go on operations [E: D2], refilled at perhaps 30–50 a year.

**Denies the enemy.** It denies the enemy's senior cadre in the South the night. From 1964 a province committee member, a regional military commander or a COSVN courier who sleeps in a hamlet that the task force's files have named can be taken from his bed by men he cannot see, in 2–6 hours from the decision [E: D5]. It denies the infrastructure the comfort that only the hamlet cadre are hunted. It denies the base areas inside the South (the Iron Triangle, the Ho Bo woods, the Do Xa, the U Minh) their freedom from observation at night. It denies the Trail and the Cambodian base areas their freedom from observation from October 1965 and September 1967, within history's limits [M014·S3]. It denies Hanoi certainty that a prisoner camp in the South is beyond reach. It does not deny the enemy its main force, its sanctuaries or its strategy.

**Verdict.** Delta is the best night raid force in the world, put into a war fought at night by an enemy who believed the night was his. That is worth something real and specific: from late 1964 the senior infrastructure in the South (province committees, regional commanders, couriers and their documents) can be taken when it is found, at night, by men who see. The unit's whole value runs through the combined task force's files [M012]. Delta adds the hands for the hardest 10–20% of the task force's targets [E: D13] and the speed to reach them before they move. That will be 50–250 more senior cadre a year at maturity, against an infrastructure counted in the tens of thousands [E: D5]. It is reconnaissance that finds the Trail and the Cambodian base areas a little better than SOG did, from history's dates. It is a better POW recovery force than any history had. It does not touch the main force, the sanctuaries or Hanoi's decision. COSVN, which the provision names, is beyond its reach until 1970 and probably after, because it was a moving headquarters of 2,400 people in a country no American could enter [M014·S7]. The raid into the North that history made, the unit could make better. It is one raid. Delta is a scalpel. The war has places to use one, and it is not won with one.

## P014b · MACV Joint Special Operations Command (MACV-JSOC), newly formed after the Gulf of Tonkin incident: a joint headquarters under COMUSMACV that commands SFOD-D and the special operations units the user will assign to it later, with standing liaison to MACV J-2 and J-3, MACV-SOG, the CIA station, the Combined Interagency Task Force of memorandum 012, the Joint General Staff and the US Mission, for logistics, targeting and deconfliction
one headquarters, formed August 1964 [U]; ~250–450 personnel [E: D2] · spaces ~250–450 [E: a joint task force headquarters at the scale of the early JSOC of 1980–81; no ceiling (CONFIG)] · arrives 1964-08-15 · FIND, FIX, STRIKE, SUSTAIN · institutional

**Key figures.**
- Formed 15 August 1964 [E: after the Tonkin reports of 2 and 4 August]; model JSOC, 15 December 1980 [M014·S8]; precedent MACV-SOG, 24 January 1964 [M014·S3]
- Strength about 250–450, of whom 40–80 in 15–20 liaison cells [E: D2]
- Liaison with MACV J-2 and J-3, SOG, the CIA station, the combined task force [M012], the air command, the four corps (US and ARVN), the JGS, the National Police, the US Mission and Vientiane [U] [E: judgment from the period's establishments and practice]
- Capacity: 2–6 operations at once, 40–150 a month; deconfliction 1–3 hours inside the South [E: D5]
- No cross-border authority; no authority over the CIA or the GVN [M014·S3] [U]
- Running cost about $10–20 million a year in 1964 prices, excluding Delta [E: judgment from the period's establishments and practice]

**Negative specification.** The headquarters cannot authorise any cross-border operation: Laos stays with the ambassador, Cambodia with Washington from September 1967, the North with the President [M014·S3] [M014·S5]. It holds no authority over the CIA, the GVN, the JGS or the National Police; it can only ask them. It brings no units except Delta, no aviation beyond Delta's own [M014·S2], no surveillance and no sources of its own: every target it acts on comes from someone else's files [M012] [M003]. It cannot stop leaks from Vietnamese channels it must use; it can only route around them. It is not a theater command, and it cannot direct the conventional war.

**Denies the enemy.** It denies the enemy the seams between the American services, SOG, the CIA station and the combined task force, which a single raid force working through MACV J-3 would leave open: fewer raids planned through channels that leak, fewer sources burned, fewer teams shot by friendly fire.

**Verdict.** The headquarters is the price of using Delta well. Without it, Delta would work through MACV J-3 and the corps, its targets would pass through hands that leak, and its raids would collide with the task force's and SOG's. With it, a small joint staff keeps the targets in American hands, clears the ground for each raid in hours, and shares what the raids bring back. It adds nothing new to the war's knowledge. It adds speed and order to a scalpel. It is also the frame for the units the user will add later, and its value will grow or shrink with them.

## Employment concepts
EC014-1 the held-belt night lift · EC014-2 the province committee take-down · EC014-3 the base-area stake-out · EC014-4 the cross-border road watch (Laos, from October 1965) · EC014-5 the Cambodian foot reconnaissance (from September 1967) · EC014-6 the camp snatch · EC014-7 the Son Tay package. Abandoned: EC014-8 the partnered ARVN cordon (cost the surprise and put the target in a Vietnamese channel) · EC014-9 the COSVN decapitation raid (no building, no border crossing, warned by trawlers) · EC014-10 the Hanoi raid (no authority) · EC014-11 the sustained hundred-raid month (no rotation base; sustained rate 25–50 raids and 8–12 recon teams)

## Interactions
- P014a × P012b: the task force's National Fusion Centre is Delta's target deck and Delta is the task force's hardest-target arm; the task force gives the raid its file, its warrant where one is possible and its exploitation team, and Delta gives the file the province and region cadre the task force's own forces could not reach (F014-1, F014-7)
- P014a × P006a: the district centres' files are the base layer under every Delta target in the South, and a raid's documents go back into them within hours (F014-1, F014-14)
- P014a × P002a: an arrest inside the held belt runs through the Special Branch and the 72-hour magistrate review of the 1964 statute, so a night raid on a house is a police action with soldiers in it; outside the held belt there is no warrant and no review, and that boundary is where Delta's political cost lives (F014-16)
- P014a × P003a, P003b: the U-2S and Global Hawk cue a team to a place worth watching, and the team sees under the canopy the imagery cannot enter; the pairing is the only instrument in the record that reaches a point target below the trees (F014-2, F014-11)
- P014a × P005a, P005b: a team's coordinate becomes a GBU-31 aimpoint through the Tan Son Nhut cell, which makes Delta the first provision that can put the J's precision on a target under canopy (F014-11)
- P014a × P013a, P013b: Delta's one possible raid into the North flies through an air-defence system that the opening strike of 2 March 1965 broke and Moscow then rebuilt; the raid is easier in 1965 and no easier in 1970 (F014-21)
- P014b × P012a: the combined operations command's corps centres clear the ground for Delta's raids and receive its restricted operating areas; without that switchboard the deconfliction would run through four American and four ARVN corps staffs one telephone call at a time (F014-6, F014-19)
- P014b × P006c: the selected advisory corps is how MACV-JSOC learns which Vietnamese channels leak, because the adviser who has been with a counterpart eighteen months is the man who knows (F014-18)
